parts.text:
(a) Find the range of these observations.
(1)

parts.label: b

(1)

(3)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Bobby calculates the following statistics from these observations

$\sum x = 23.72 \qquad \sum x^2 = 13.4228$

(d) Show that the standard deviation of these observations is 0.176 to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: e(i)
parts.text:
Bobby now collects 18 more observations, $y$, from the same investigation.

(e) Using all 65 observations, the sample mean is 0.502 and the sample standard deviation is 0.204

(i) Show that $\sum y = 8.91$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(e)(i) M1: $\frac{\sum y + 23.72}{65}=0.502$ or $0.502\times 65=32.63$
A1*: $32.63=\sum y +23.72$, so $\sum y = 8.91$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: For a correct equation for sample mean or for $0.502\times 65$ (implied by 32.63 seen)

parts.label: e(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) Showing your working, calculate $\sum y^2$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(ii) M1: $0.204=\sqrt{\frac{13.4228+\sum y^2}{65}-0.502^2}$ or $0.204^2=\frac{13.4228+\sum y^2}{65}-0.502^2$
M1: $\sum y^2 = (0.204^2+0.502^2)\times 65 -13.4228$
A1: $=5.6625$, awrt $5.66$
Official notes (completeness pass):

- A1: awrt 5.66  (SC attempting to use $s$ gives 5.62  send to review)

questions.stem:
A factory makes rugs and blankets from wool **or** cotton **or** polyester.

• 30% of the items made are rugs and 70% of the items made are blankets

• 60% of the rugs are made from wool

• 35% of the blankets are made from wool

• 10% of the rugs are made from cotton

• 20% of the blankets are made from cotton

• the rest of the rugs and blankets are made from polyester

An item made by the factory is selected at random.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Complete the tree diagram below to illustrate this information.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: Rug branch probabilities $0.6$ (wool), $0.1$ (cotton), $0.3$ (polyester)
B1: Blanket branch probabilities $0.35$ (wool), $0.2$ (cotton), $0.45$ (polyester)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1: At least 5 probabilities correct  (allow fraction, percentage or decimal) But do not allow eg $\frac{3.5}{10}$ or 35 (without percentage symbol)
- B1: All 8 probabilities correct  (allow fraction, percentage or decimal) But do not allow eg $\frac{3.5}{10}$ or 35 (without percentage symbol)

parts.label: b(i)
parts.text:
(b) (i) Find the probability that the item selected is **not** made from wool.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b)(i) M1: $\mathrm{P}(W')=0.3\times(0.1+0.3)+0.7\times(0.2+0.45)$ or $\mathrm{P}(W')=1-(0.3\times0.6+0.7\times0.35)$
A1: $=0.575$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Correct probability expression ft the probabilities from their part (a)
- A1: $\frac{23}{40}$ oe  allow equivalent fraction, decimal or percentage

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) Given that this item is **not** made from wool, find the probability that it is a blanket.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(ii) M1: $\mathrm{P}(B\mid W')=\frac{\mathrm{P}(B\cap W')}{\mathrm{P}(W')}=\frac{0.7\times(0.2+0.45)}{'0.575'}$
A1: $=\frac{91}{115}$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Correct method for conditional probability used  ft their part (a) and ft their (b)(i)
- A1: awrt 0.791  allow awrt 79.1%

questions.stem:
A manufacturer of pet food gives samples of three new flavours of cat food, $A$, $B$ and $C$, to each of 100 customers who each own one cat. These customers are surveyed to find out whether or not their cat likes each flavour with the following results

40 cats like $A$

45 cats like $B$

50 cats like $C$

19 cats like both $A$ and $B$

20 cats like both $A$ and $C$

22 cats like both $B$ and $C$

12 cats like all three of these flavours.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Using these results complete the Venn diagram below.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: 12 correct in the centre of the Venn diagram
B1: At least two of 7, 8 and 10 correct
B1ft: Any one of 13, 16 or 20 correct ft their 7, 8, 10 and 12 (must be positive) such that the 4 regions of $A=40$ or the 4 regions of $B=45$ or the 4 regions of $C=50$
B1: All correct including the 14
Official notes (completeness pass):
- In part (a) allow the numbers in the Venn diagram written as probabilities eg 0.12, 0.07, 0.08 etc.
- B1ft: Do not accept blank regions as 0 for ft.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
For these cats,

(b) determine whether or not a cat liking flavour $A$ is independent of it liking flavour $C$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: Labelling all of the probabilities needed for a test of independence (probabilities must be correct or ft from their Venn diagram). Must use $A$ and $C$.
Either $\mathrm{P}(A),\mathrm{P}(C)$ and $\mathrm{P}(A\cap C)$: $\mathrm{P}(A)=\frac{40}{100}$, $\mathrm{P}(C)=\frac{50}{100}$, $\mathrm{P}(A\cap C)=\frac{20}{100}$
or $\mathrm{P}(A)$ and $\mathrm{P}(A\mid C)$: $\mathrm{P}(A)=\frac{40}{100}$, $\mathrm{P}(A\mid C)=\frac{20}{50}$
A1: Stating correct test with correct values $\mathrm{P}(A)\times \mathrm{P}(C)=\mathrm{P}(A\cap C)$ or $\mathrm{P}(A)=\mathrm{P}(A\mid C)$ and correct conclusion of independence

parts.label: c(i)
parts.text:
(c) One of these 100 cats is chosen at random.

(i) Find the probability that it likes only one of the three flavours.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c)(i) B1ft: $\left[\frac{'13'+'16'+'20'}{100}\right]=\frac{49}{100}$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1ft: Ft their “13”, “16” and “20” provided the answer is a probability

parts.label: c(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) Given that it likes flavour $C$, find the probability that it also likes flavour $B$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(ii) M1: $\mathrm{P}(\text{likes } B\mid \text{likes } C)=\frac{'12'+'10'}{'12'+'10'+'8'+'20'}$
A1: $=\frac{22}{50}$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Correct method for conditional probability using all appropriate regions of their Venn Diagram. Condone $\frac{n}{50}$ (provided it does not come from simplification of $\frac{2n}{100}$) or $\frac{\frac{n}{100}}{\frac{50}{100}}$ with $n\leqslant 34$. $\frac{\frac{22}{100}}{\frac{50}{100}}$ scores M1. Assuming independence is M0 eg $\frac{\frac{45}{100}\times\frac{50}{100}}{\frac{50}{100}}$
- A1: 0.44 oe

questions.stem:
A recycling centre measures the weight of glass deposited by the public each day.

The weight of glass, $S$ kg, deposited at the recycling centre in a day during the summer can be modelled by $S\sim \mathrm{N}(700, 50^2)$

parts.label: a(i)
parts.text:
(a) Using standardisation and showing your working, find the probability that, in one randomly selected day during the summer,

(i) more than 640 kg of glass is deposited at the recycling centre,
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a)(i) M1: $\mathrm{P}(S>640)=\mathrm{P}\left(Z>\frac{640-700}{50}\right)$
A1: awrt $0.885$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Attempt to standardise with 640, 700 and 50  allow $\pm$  (not implied by $\pm$1.2 on its own)
- A1: awrt 0.885 (calc gives 0.884930…)  answer only is M0A0 must see standardisation. do not isw if 1 – 0.8849 is then found

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) 700 kg of glass, correct to the nearest 50 kg, is deposited at the recycling centre.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(ii) M1: $675<S<725$
M1: $\mathrm{P}(675<S<725)=\mathrm{P}(S<725)-\mathrm{P}(S<675)$ **or** use of symmetry to find correct area
M1: $\mathrm{P}(S<725)=\mathrm{P}\left(Z<\frac{725-700}{50}\right)$ **or** $\mathrm{P}(S<675)=\mathrm{P}\left(Z<\frac{675-700}{50}\right)$
A1: $\mathrm{P}(-0.5<Z<0.5)=0.6915-(1-0.6915)$ or $1-2\times0.3085$ or $2\times(0.6915-0.5)$
A1: $=0.383$, awrt $0.383$

SC: Use of 650 and 750 scores a maximum of 4 out of 5 [must be 650 **and** 750 to apply SC].
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Sight of 675 or 725
- M1: Use of $\mathrm{P}(675<S<g)=\mathrm{P}(S<g)-\mathrm{P}(S<675)$ where $724\leqslant g\leqslant 725$ or correct use of symmetry eg $\mathrm{P}(675<S<725)=2(\mathrm{P}(S<725)-0.5)$ or eg $\mathrm{P}(675<S<725)=1-2\mathrm{P}(S<675)$
- M1: One correct standardisation seen of 675 or $g$ with 700 and 50  where $724\leqslant g\leqslant 725$. Allow for just $\pm$0.5 oe seen as a $z$-value (not a probability)
- A1: (dep on 3rd M1) sight of awrt 0.69 or awrt 0.31
- A1: (dep on 3rd M1) awrt 0.383
- SC Use of 650 and 750: M0. M1 Use of $\mathrm{P}(650<S<750)=\mathrm{P}(S<750)-\mathrm{P}(S<650)$ or use of symmetry to find correct area. M1 standardising 650 or 750 with 700 and 50 or just $\pm$1 seen as a $z$–value (not a probability). A1 (dep on 3rd M1) sight of awrt 0.84 or awrt 0.16. A1 (dep on 3rd M1) awrt 0.683

parts.label: b(i)
parts.text:
The weight of glass, $W$ kg, deposited at the recycling centre in a day during the winter can be modelled by $W\sim \mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$

(b) Given that $\mathrm{P}(W>680)=0.0668$ and $\mathrm{P}(W<599)=0.3$

(i) find **two** equations in terms of $\mu$ and $\sigma$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b)(i) M1A1: $\frac{680-\mu}{\sigma}=1.5$
A1: $\frac{599-\mu}{\sigma}=-0.5244$
Official notes (completeness pass):

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) Hence, showing your working, find the value of $\mu$ and the value of $\sigma$
(3)

questions.stem:
A farmer supplies cabbages to a local supermarket. The supermarket manager takes a random sample of 200 of these cabbages and the weight of each cabbage is recorded.

The weights of the cabbages in the sample are summarised in the following box plot.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Use linear interpolation to estimate the probability that a randomly chosen cabbage from this sample has a weight of less than 570 grams.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: $\mathrm{P}(C<570)=0.5+\frac{570-550}{650-550}\times0.25$ or $\frac{x-100}{150-100}=\frac{570-550}{650-550}$
A1: $=0.55$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Correct method $0.5+p\times 0.25$ where $0<p<1$ or attempt to find the number of cabbages weighing less than 570 (implied by $x$ = 110)
- A1: 0.55  condone awrt 0.55 for 2 out of 2 marks

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The supermarket manager takes the quartiles from this sample and now decides to classify any cabbage whose weight is at least $Q_3+1.5\times(Q_3-Q_1)$ as extra-large.

(b) Find the minimum weight of a cabbage that the supermarket manager would classify as extra-large.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) B1: $Q_3+1.5\times(Q_3-Q_1)=650+1.5\times200$ $=950$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1: cao

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The supermarket manager assumes that the weights of cabbages supplied to the supermarket may be modelled by a normal distribution.

(c) Explain whether or not the box plot supports this assumption.
(1)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
The farmer records the weight of every cabbage harvested from a field and classifies any cabbage whose weight is more than 2 standard deviations above the mean as an outlier.

Assuming that the weights of the cabbages from this field may be modelled by a normal distribution,

(d) find the probability that a randomly selected cabbage harvested from the field would be classified as an outlier using the farmer's method.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) M1: $z=2$, $\mathrm{P}(Z>2)[=1-0.9772]$
A1: $=0.0228$

- A1: awrt 0.0228 (calculator gives 0.0227501…)

Given that a cabbage with a weight of 1000 grams is classified as an outlier by the farmer,

(e) find the maximum possible value of the standard deviation of the weights of cabbages harvested from the field.
